1. # ***Introduction*** {#introduction}

This strategic plan has been prepared to guide the operations of CSPARK over the period 2020 – 2025\. 

CSPARK is a Non-Governmental Organisation that is duly registered under Section 10 of the NGOs Co-ordination Act, 1990 of Kenya (Reg. Number: OP.218/051/19-325/11713). Its key focus is on bridging the gap between spatial planning and social justice. This focus is informed by the recognition that while various state institutions have been carrying out spatial planning, often, these plans remain unimplemented and largely out of touch with the general populace. In fact, these plans are sometimes the very triggers of the widening social inequality and its attendant challenges. The mismatch between spatial planning and its desired outcomes therefore not only engenders social inequality; it also widens it, thereby aggravating social injustice. 

Social injustice in the Global South is compounded by emerging challenges of poverty, climate change, rising cases of lifestyle diseases, food insecurity, social polarisation, gender inequality, water scarcity, use of energy from non-renewable sources and growing demand for cheap energy, weak industrial base to sustain urbanisation witnessed in the region, and inefficient management of shared resources. 

Tackling the above concerns lies at the heart of the shared visions and goals contained in the Sustainable Development Goals and the New Urban Agenda. Kenya has undertaken ambitious legal reforms and crafted a number of development strategies to domesticate these shared visions and goals. Among these are The Kenya Constitution of 2010, the Kenya Vision 2030, Urban Areas and Cities Act, the Big Four Agenda, and the Urban Development Policy. 

However, whereas spatial planning forms an integrative approach through which the visions and targets can be realised, its present form of practice and the legal mandates of the bodies charged with activities that have a bearing on spatial planning in the country inhibit its ability to make its rightful contribution in solving the challenges. The result of this situation is disjointed planning whose implication is to aggravate spatial injustice. CSPARK endeavours to adopt an integrated approach to bridging this gap by availing research-based evidence for undertaking spatial planning as well as technical expertise to tackle the issues.

2. # ***Our Vision, mission, and the core values***  {#our-vision,-mission,-and-the-core-values}

## ***Vision Statement*** {#vision-statement}

Integrated spatial planning that delivers social justice.

## ***Mission Statement***  {#mission-statement}

To link spatial planning to social justice through research, advocacy and capacity development.

## ***Values*** {#values}

The core values of CSPARK will guide not only its relation with its partners but also its own work culture. Among our core values are: that will be guided by the following core values: 

1. Broad-based stakeholder participation and teamwork  
2. Integrity in all our researches, operations, and dealings  
3. Respect for gender, cultural, and socio-economic diversity   
4. Upholding the best interest of society at large  
5. Financial and social accountability to our partners and the society  

3. # ***Campaigning the Cause*** {#campaigning-the-cause}

CSPARK believes that it is possible to achieve social justice through informed and responsive spatial planning. This belief notwithstanding, there exists a gap in the manner in which spatial planning is currently undertaken, majorly by the state organs. Due to their legal mandates and institutional inertia, these state organs have ended up producing plans which are either rigid or simply produced as an end in itself and therefore have little bearing in helping address the plight of the most vulnerable in the society. CSPARK beliefs that it is possible to make these plans useful for the socio-economic transformation that spatial planning strives to achieve. As such, it strives to partner with both state and non-state actors and to leverage its strength to bridge the current gap between spatial planning, implementation, and social justice. To this end, CSPARK will avail its expertise in research, stakeholder engagement, spatial planning, governance, and reach out to like-minded institutions to provide other resources that are needed to achieve social justice through spatial planning. The organisation will carry out researches to find out the concerns that spatial planning needs to pay attention to and also rally the implementing agencies to initiate projects that address these concerns. 

4. # ***Goals and Tasks*** {#goals-and-tasks}

The following are the goals and tasks that CSPARK shall pursue in the next five years:

1) Spatial planning and spatial governance  
   1. Research and advocate for the implementation of innovative planning standards that focus on the operationalisation of Code 95 for the benefit of the poor and residents of five informal settlements, preparation of three Local Economic Development Plans, three Integrated Strategic Urban Development Plans, three Integrated Development Plans, and one land reorganisation plan  
   2. Advocate for the implementation of adoptive planning standards in 5 towns  
   3. Conduct research on Marine spatial planning around Lake Victoria and Indian Ocean and prepare two such plans  
   4. Preparation of three plans to guide rural development in Kisii, Siaya and Makueni   
   5. Carry out an evaluative study of the impacts of existing urban development plans on the development of the urban areas/ cities   
   6. Develop a framework for participatory land governance to guide the operationalisation of Community Land Act and sedentarisation among the pastoralist communities  
   7. Develop innovative land tenure models e.g. communal land trust to respond to challenges such as housing   
   8. Offer technical backstopping for setting up and operationalising urban management boards five boards, preparing five strategic plans and training of members of five urban management boards  
   9. Conduct researches to explore the possibilities of increasing municipal revenue base through the land value capture, user charges, transfer of development rights, development charges  
2) Urban livelihoods   
   1. Carry out participatory enumeration of street traders in Nakuru, Eldoret, Wote, Nairobi, and Mombasa  
   2. Offer technical backstopping for participatory planning of four urban markets in Nakuru, Eldoret, Wote, Nairobi, and Mombasa  
3) Urban infrastructure   
   1. Develop a framework for participatory solid waste management in two neighbourhoods in Wote, Nairobi and Kisumu  
   2. Conduct researches and develop policies for the recognition of invisible modes of co-production of urban services and infrastructure to make them visible to policy makers \# Conduct researches and develop policies for the recognition of the role of informal sector in extending water infrastructure beyond municipal networks  
   3. Conduct researches to understand mobility patterns and behaviours in Nairobi and Kisumu and lobby for the linking of this knowledge to the new transport infrastructure and services projects  
   4. Develop a policy framework for linking informal modes of transport to the formal modes in Kisumu, Mombasa and Wote  
   5. Develop County Green Energy Plans for Kisumu, Uasin Gishu, Mombasa and Makueni and advocate for clean energy   
   6. Carry out research to inform the urban energy transitions from use of traditional energy sources to more efficient energy modes   
   7. Conduct research to find out the impacts of prepaid citizenship on those living in areas that rely on negotiated settlement of energy bills arrangement   
4) Urban housing  
   1. Carry out participatory enumeration and mapping of informal settlements  
   2. Develop Relocation Action Plans to assist in affordable housing projects and informal settlements upgrading  
   3. Conduct researches to understand the socio-economic enhancements for the vulnerable populations  
   4. Develop a policy framework for linking the vulnerable to livelihoods, crime and informal settlements, socio-economic needs of the informal settlements to informal settlements upgrading processes   
5) Urban security   
   1. Carry out research and lobby for the improvement of neighbourhood security through address system that builds on the *nyumba* *kumi* initiative, neighbourhood associations, residents associations and formal security systems

6. # ***Human Resources*** {#human-resources}

The organisation shall be headed by an Executive Director, who shall be directly answerable to the Board of Directors. There shall also be an internal auditor and a monitoring and evaluation officer. Other staff members shall include the directors of research, advocacy and lobbying, programmes and corporate services. 

The organisation will need an office assistant and two research assistants in its first six months of operation as it stabilises. During this period, other research assistants will be engaged as need arises. Additional research assistants will be engaged on a more long-term basis as need arises. In house training will be carried out for the research assistants in the next three years to enable them upgrade their skills and be in a position to manage projects on their own as the organisation grows.

Basic book keeping and auditing services will be handled by internal audit expertise. However, an independent auditor and finance advisor will be engaged to ensure that the books of the organisation are in order.

The organisation will also engage a driver who will double up as the support staff in the immediate term. The number of drivers and support staff is expected to increase as the organisation grows bigger. 

The organisation shall draw on the diverse expertise and experience of the following individuals to steer its operations.

7. # ***The Management Structure*** {#the-management-structure}

The organisation shall adopt the structure shown Figure 7-1.

![][image1]  
*Figure 7-1: Management structure of CSPARK*

## ***The Board of Directors*** {#the-board-of-directors}

The Board of Directors shall be the supreme decision-making organ of the organisation. 

## ***Number of Directors***  {#number-of-directors}

The Board shall be the policy organ and shall unless otherwise varied by a special resolution passed at a general meeting the Board consist of a minimum of Five (5) and a maximum of nine (9) members, three of whom will fill the honorary posts of Chairman, Secretary and Treasurer. In instances where the Chairman is absent, the Board members can elect one of their own to act in that position; the Chief Executive Officer shall be the secretary to the Board.

The Chief Executive Officer shall head the secretariat and shall be assisted by the employees of the Organisation to manage the day-to-day affairs of the Organisation.  The management may pay all expenses incurred in setting up and registering the Organisation and may exercise such powers of the Organisation as are required by the constitution to be exercised to achieve the objectives of the Organisation. No regulations made by the Organisation in a General Meeting shall invalidate any prior act of the management, which would have been valid, if such regulations had not been made. 

The Chief Executive Officer shall be shall be an ex officio member of the Board. 

## ***Duties of the Board***  {#duties-of-the-board}

1. The Board will appoint and remove Directors by way of a formal resolution that is duly passed at a properly constituted meeting of the Board.   
   2. A resolution shall be put by the Chair at each annual General Meeting of Members to confirm the decisions made under clause 12.2 by the Board since the previous annual General Meeting.  
   3. The Board may exercise all those powers of the Organization as are not, by this Constitution, required to be exercised by the Members in General Meeting or otherwise.

8. # ***SWOT Analysis*** {#swot-analysis}

The organisation will have to overcome its weaknesses and threats facing it with its strengths and opportunities.

## ***Strengths***  {#strengths}

These include the following: 

1) Diverse work experience and qualifications of its leadership   
2) Teamwork among the leaders   
3) Common vision shared by the leaders

## ***Weaknesses***  {#weaknesses}

1) Relatively a new organisation

## ***Opportunities***  {#opportunities}

1) Few organisation approach spatial planning from the perspective of the organisation  
2) Legal reforms that support the need for spatial planning in Kenya  
3) New spatial planning concerns raised by the global climate change phenomenon, gender awareness, sedenterisation of pastoralist communities, growing social inequality, COVID-19 pandemic  
4) Clear development visions and goals spelt out by the Sustainable Development Goals, New Urban Agenda, Kenya Vision 2030, Kenya’s Urban Development Policy  
5) Recognition and expansion of basic human rights by the Kenyan Constitution  
6) Devolved government structure under the Kenyan Constitution 2010

## ***Threats***  {#threats}

1) Government regulations   
2) Slow economic performance occasioned by new threats such as the COVID-19 pandemic 

It is important to strategise in order to overcome the above weaknesses and threats. To deal with the threats, the organisation will focus its work on helping communities overcome the challenges posed by the new threats such as the COVID-19 pandemic. In terms of its relatively young age, the organisation will emphasise on the work experience and qualifications of the members that comprise it rather than the organisation itself. While the organisation itself is relatively young, its members are seasoned in diverse areas of expertise.
